subject: physics
title: Particle model and pressure
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: Particle model and pressure — AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification, section 4.3.3.
meta_desc: GCSE Physics (AQA) practice covering Particle model and pressure, specification section 4.3.3.
final_note: You worked through Particle model and pressure — 16 specification statements.

concepts.def: The molecules of a gas are in constant random motion. They travel in all directions and at a wide range of speeds, changing direction whenever they collide with one another or with the walls of the container. No molecule keeps one path or one speed for long.

The temperature of a gas is related to the average kinetic energy of the molecules. A higher temperature means a higher average kinetic energy, so the molecules move faster on average. It is an average across the whole gas: at any instant some molecules are moving much faster than others.

Gas molecules collide with the walls of the container. Each collision exerts a small force on the wall, and the pressure is the total force these collisions exert on each unit area of wall. Anything that makes the collisions more frequent, or makes each collision exert a greater force, increases the pressure.

concepts.term: Temperature and pressure at constant volume
concepts.def: Changing the temperature of a gas, held at constant volume, changes the pressure exerted by the gas. Raising the temperature raises the average kinetic energy of the molecules, so they move faster: they strike the walls more often each second and each strike exerts a greater force, so the pressure rises. Cooling the gas does the reverse and the pressure falls.

The gas is sealed in a container whose size cannot change, such as a rigid metal can or a sealed glass flask. The gas cannot expand or contract, so any change in the pressure must come from a change in the motion of the molecules.

The pressure of a gas produces a net force at right angles to the wall of the gas container, or to any surface placed in the gas. Individual molecules arrive at the surface from all directions, but the sideways parts of their impacts cancel out, leaving a combined force perpendicular to the surface.

concepts.term: Compression and expansion of a gas
concepts.def: A gas can be compressed or expanded by pressure changes. Increasing the pressure acting on a gas squashes it into a smaller volume; reducing the pressure allows it to expand into a larger volume.

If the volume in which a fixed mass of gas is contained is increased while the temperature stays constant, the same number of molecules is spread through a larger space. The molecules travel further between hits on the walls, so each area of wall is struck less often each second and the pressure decreases. The molecules do not change speed, because the temperature has not changed.

concepts.term: Fixed mass held at a constant temperature
concepts.def: The conditions under which pressure × volume = constant applies. The gas must be sealed so that no molecules enter or leave it (a fixed mass), and its temperature must not change during the compression or expansion. If either condition is broken, the product of pressure and volume is no longer constant.

For a fixed mass of gas held at a constant temperature: pressure × volume = constant [p V = constant], where pressure, p, is in pascals, Pa, and volume, V, is in metres cubed, m^3. Multiplying the pressure by the volume gives the same value before and after the change.
The unit of pressure. In p V = constant the pressure, p, is in pascals, Pa. A pressure in any other unit must be converted to pascals before the equation is used.

The unit of volume. In p V = constant the volume, V, is in metres cubed, m^3. A volume measured in cm^3 must be converted first, because 1 m^3 = 1 000 000 cm^3, so a volume in cm^3 is divided by 1 000 000 to give m^3.

concepts.term: Calculating a change in pressure or volume
concepts.def: For a fixed mass of gas held at constant temperature the product p × V has the same value before and after a change. So multiply the starting pressure by the starting volume to find that constant, then divide it by the new volume to find the new pressure, or by the new pressure to find the new volume. Squeezing the gas into a smaller volume must give a larger pressure, and letting it expand must give a smaller one — a useful check on the answer.

Work is the transfer of energy by a force. When a force moves the object it acts on, energy is transferred, and that transfer is the work done. Work is a transfer of energy, not a store of energy that something holds.

Doing work on a gas increases the internal energy of the gas and can cause an increase in the temperature of the gas. The energy reaches the gas because a force pushes it and moves it, not because the gas has been heated by something hotter.

The energy stored inside the gas by its molecules — the total kinetic and potential energy of all of them. Increasing the internal energy of a gas by doing work on it raises the average kinetic energy of its molecules, and since temperature is related to that average kinetic energy, the temperature of the gas can rise.

concepts.term: Doing work on the gas in a bicycle pump
concepts.def: When the piston of a bicycle pump is pushed in, the piston exerts a force on the enclosed gas and moves it, so work is done on the gas. Energy is transferred to the gas, its internal energy increases, the average kinetic energy of its molecules increases and the temperature of the gas rises — which is why the barrel of the pump becomes noticeably warm after several strokes.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly describes the molecules of a gas and what the temperature of the gas tells you?
options: They are in constant random motion, and the temperature is related to their average kinetic energy.
They all travel at one fixed speed, and the temperature is related to that single shared speed.
They are in constant random motion, and the temperature is related to the total kinetic energy of the gas.
They move along fixed paths, and the temperature is related to how far apart the molecules are.
mcqs.explain: This is exactly what the specification states: the molecules are in constant random motion, and the temperature of the gas is related to the average kinetic energy of the molecules.

mcqs.q: A sealed metal can holds a gas. The can is rigid, so the volume of the gas cannot change. The can is warmed gently. Why does the pressure of the gas rise?
options: The molecules themselves swell as they warm, so they press more tightly on the walls.
The molecules strike the walls harder, but the number of strikes each second is unchanged.
The molecules gain kinetic energy, so they strike the walls harder and more often each second.
Warming makes the gas expand inside the can, and the expanding gas pushes on the walls.
mcqs.explain: Raising the temperature raises the average kinetic energy of the molecules; faster molecules collide with the walls both more frequently and with greater force, so the pressure rises.

mcqs.q: What causes the pressure that a gas exerts on the wall of its container?
options: The weight of the gas pressing down on the wall, because gravity pulls the gas downwards.
The molecules repelling one another, pushing the outer ones firmly against the wall.
Molecules sliding along the wall, dragging on it in their own direction of travel.
Molecules colliding with the wall, each collision exerting a small force on the wall.
mcqs.explain: Gas pressure is the combined effect of enormous numbers of molecular collisions with the wall, each exerting a small force over the area of the wall.

mcqs.q: A fixed mass of gas is sealed in a rigid container, so its volume is constant. Its temperature is lowered. What happens to the pressure of the gas, and why?
options: It stays the same, because the volume of the container has not been changed.
It falls, because the cooled molecules shrink and so press less on the walls.
It falls, because slower molecules hit the walls less often and with less force.
It falls, because the molecules hit the walls with less force but just as often.
mcqs.explain: Cooling lowers the average kinetic energy, so the molecules move more slowly: they reach the walls less frequently and each collision exerts a smaller force, so the pressure falls.

mcqs.q: A flat plate is held inside a container of gas. In which direction does the gas pressure produce a net force on the plate?
options: A net force straight downwards on the surface.
A net force slanted along the surface it strikes.
A net force spread evenly in every direction at once.
A net force at right angles to the surface.
mcqs.explain: The specification states that the pressure produces a net force at right angles to the wall of the gas container (or any surface); the sideways parts of the impacts cancel.

mcqs.q: A sealed syringe contains a fixed mass of gas. The plunger is pulled out very slowly, so the temperature of the gas stays constant. Using the particle model, why does the pressure of the gas decrease?
options: The molecules slow down when given more room, so each strike on the wall is weaker.
The molecules are further apart, so they collide with one another far less often.
The gas becomes thinner, so there is now less gas available to push on the walls.
The molecules spread through a bigger volume, so fewer hit each area of wall per second.
mcqs.explain: The same molecules, at the same average speed, travel further between collisions with the walls, so each area of wall is struck less often each second and the pressure falls.

mcqs.q: Under which conditions does pressure × volume = constant apply to a gas?
options: For any gas whose temperature is changing but whose mass is fixed.
For a fixed mass of gas held at a constant temperature.
For a fixed mass of gas held in a container of constant volume.
For any gas in which the pressure and the volume increase together.
mcqs.explain: These are exactly the conditions the specification states before giving pressure × volume = constant.

mcqs.q: A fixed mass of gas is held at a constant temperature. For this gas, p V = 24 (with p in Pa and V in m^3). Which pair of readings is possible for this gas?
options: p = 6 Pa, V = 4 m^3
p = 3 Pa, V = 2 m^3
mcqs.explain: 6 × 4 = 24, so this pair gives the required constant value of pressure × volume.

mcqs.q: Which units must be used for pressure and volume in the equation p V = constant?
options: pressure in newtons, volume in metres cubed
pressure in pascals, volume in centimetres cubed
pressure in pascals, volume in metres cubed
pressure in newtons, volume in centimetres cubed
mcqs.explain: The specification states pressure, p, in pascals, Pa, and volume, V, in metres cubed, m^3.

mcqs.q: A sealed container holds a gas in a volume of 5000 cm^3. What is this volume in the unit required by the equation p V = constant?
A fixed mass of gas at a constant temperature has a volume of 0.020 m^3 at a pressure of 150 000 Pa. It is compressed to a volume of 0.005 m^3. What is the new pressure of the gas?
mcqs.explain: pV = 150 000 × 0.020 = 3000. The new pressure is 3000 ÷ 0.005 = 600 000 Pa — four times larger, as the volume is four times smaller.

mcqs.q: A fixed mass of gas at a constant temperature has a volume of 0.60 m^3 at a pressure of 200 000 Pa. The pressure is reduced to 50 000 Pa. What is the new volume of the gas?
mcqs.explain: pV = 200 000 × 0.60 = 120 000. The new volume is 120 000 ÷ 50 000 = 2.4 m^3 — four times larger, as the pressure is four times smaller.

mcqs.q: In physics, what is meant by work?
options: Work is the transfer of energy by heating a gas.
Work is the transfer of energy by a force.
Work is the energy stored inside a squashed gas.
Work is the force needed to move an object.
mcqs.explain: This is the specification's definition exactly: work is the transfer of energy by a force.

mcqs.q: A gas is squashed quickly inside a sealed, well-insulated container, so no energy is transferred to it by heating. What happens to the gas?
options: Nothing changes its energy, because no energy is transferred by heating.
Its temperature rises, but the internal energy of the gas stays the same.
Work is done on it, so its internal energy rises and it can get hotter.
Its internal energy falls, because energy is used up squashing the gas.
mcqs.explain: Doing work on a gas increases the internal energy of the gas and can cause an increase in the temperature of the gas — no heating is needed.

mcqs.q: After a tyre has been inflated, the barrel of the bicycle pump is noticeably warm — warmer than the tyre and warmer than the hands holding it. What is the best explanation?
options: Friction between the piston and barrel is the only cause of the warming.
The piston does work on the gas, raising its internal energy and temperature.
Heat flows into the pump from the tyre and from the hands holding it.
The gas temperature rises although its internal energy does not change.
mcqs.explain: The force on the piston moves the enclosed gas, so work is done on it. Its internal energy increases, the average kinetic energy of its molecules increases and its temperature rises.
